content: Acupuncture has been traditionally utilized in China as a treatment for asthma and is increasingly being adopted for this purpose in other parts of the world. The aim of this review was to evaluate the effects of acupuncture in managing asthma or asthma-like symptoms. To gather relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register (last searched in August 2008), the Cochrane Complementary Medicine Field trials register, AMED, and reference lists of related articles. Additionally, researchers and trialists in the field of complementary and alternative medicine were contacted for further information. The review included randomized and potentially randomized trials that employed needle acupuncture or other forms of acupuncture stimulation. Any type of control treatment was considered acceptable, including no additional treatment beyond conventional asthma management, sham or placebo interventions, and active comparator interventions. Studies were included if they assessed outcomes at least one week after the intervention. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by at least two reviewers. An acupuncture expert evaluated the appropriateness of both the active and sham acupuncture methods used in the studies. Study authors were contacted to provide any missing data. A total of 12 studies, involving 350 participants, met the inclusion criteria. However, the quality of trial reporting was poor, and the overall quality of the studies was deemed insufficient to draw generalizable conclusions. There was significant variability in the types of active and sham acupuncture used, the outcomes measured, and the time points at which these outcomes were assessed. Notably, some of the acupuncture points used in the sham arms of certain studies are traditionally considered effective for asthma treatment in Chinese medicine. Two studies employed individualized acupuncture treatment strategies, while one study used a combination of formula acupuncture with additional individualized points. No statistically significant or clinically meaningful effects of acupuncture were observed when compared to sham acupuncture. For example, pooled data from two small studies assessing lung function (post-treatment FEV1) showed a Standardized Mean Difference of 0.12, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -0.31 to 0.55, indicating no significant benefit. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to make definitive recommendations regarding the use of acupuncture for asthma treatment. Future research should address the complexities of acupuncture and explore the various types and approaches to this intervention.
